about: CK-M, the Modeler checkpoint: an unseen problem in two variants (a water utility's pumping LP, or an analysis of Prairie Town's 2025 year), a supplied model with one planted defect, and a validation against an independent reference. Every number and brief is illustrative except the 2025 SPP shapes (town_year.json, EIA-930) and EIA's 2025 capacity factors. The course's tests solve every model with the same HiGHS build the page uses and check every answer below.
intro: Eleven tasks in three parts, about 240 minutes: A, the brief (about 120); B, the planted defect (about 60); C, a validation (about 45); then submit (about 15).

The level: at least 6 of the 9 auto-marked tasks right on the first try, including all three of part B (tasks 6 to 8), for Proficient; 8 of 9 and every written point for Strong. Each number task states its tolerance.

No hints. Each task's worked solution opens after your first answer; two wait until the tasks whose answers they name are answered too. A task whose solution you open before answering counts as not right (a written task: no points); opening the full worked solutions before all eleven tasks are answered makes the attempt practice, with no level.
A written task stays as you first submit it: that is the text you rate.
Work in the starter notebook and enter your results here. Your answers stay in this browser; “Copy my results” gives a summary to share, including what you typed.

brief.text: Prairie Town's water utility pumps groundwater into a water tower, and the town draws its water from the tower. Find tomorrow's pumping schedule that meets the town's water use at the least electricity cost for the day.
facts: Water use
forecast for each hour of tomorrow, in the table below (m³)
Pumps
lift up to 900 m³ an hour and use 0.5 kWh of electricity per m³ pumped
Tower
holds 800 to 4,000 m³; 2,000 m³ at the start of the day, and at least as much at the end
Energy price
the rural electric co-op's time-of-use price: $0.06 per kWh from 22:00 to 06:00, $0.20 from 16:00 to 21:00, $0.10 otherwise
Demand charge
$0.40 for each kW of the day's highest hourly draw
brief.note: All numbers in this brief are illustrative.

empirical.text: How far can Prairie Town count on its wind and solar farms when it needs power most? Report what it can and cannot count on, and how far that depends on the dataset's scaling.
facts: Data
town_year.json, the course's year file: the real 2025 hourly demand, wind and solar of the Southwest Power Pool grid (EIA-930), each as a shape in thousandths of its own highest 2025 hour
Metadata
the file's meta block gives the source, the time convention and how bad hours were filled
Scaling
as lesson 0: demand × 450 MW, the wind farm × 150 MW, the solar farm × 200 MW, so SPP's highest hour means a farm at its full size
Compare
each farm's output in the 100 hours of highest demand, and in the 100 hours of highest net load (demand minus wind and solar), with its average over the year
Ties
where hours tie, take the earlier one first

sppWind.about: The like-for-like wind benchmark: the Southwest Power Pool's (balancing authority SWPP) 2025 wind output over its wind capacity counted as EIA counts it. Capacity: EIA's monthly generator inventory, units with Status (OP) Operating and Technology Onshore Wind Turbine; time-adjusted net summer capacity by the rule of EIA's Electric Power Monthly Table 6.07.B (each month the units in operation for the whole month; the year the hour-weighted average). Output: EIA-930 adjusted wind, cleaned as the course's year file is (671 hours of frozen telemetry replaced by the same hour on nearby valid days; no missing hours).

file.derivedBy: the course's EIA-860M extraction step (onshore wind units of SWPP in operation, by month)

sppWind.outputDerivedBy: the same extraction step on the EIA-930 files, with the cleaning rules of the course's year file (town_year.json)

defect.about: The supplied model: what should Prairie Town build (wind, solar, a gas [[combined-cycle|combined-cycle plant]], a gas [[peaker|peaker]]) to meet demand on three representative days of 2025, each weighted by the days of the year it stands for? One planted defect.
notes: illustrative round numbers: capital already annualized ($ per MW of capacity per year); running costs as in lesson 0
the three real days' SPP shape × 450 MW
output per MW built: the SPP shapes scaled to EIA's 2025 U.S. capacity factors (33.8% and 24.0%) with the course's scale method
paper: w_d = the days of the year that day d stands for (121, 122, 122; they sum to 365).
min Σ_g A_g K_g + Σ_d w_d Σ_t [ (Σ_g c_g p_g,d,t) + V u_d,t ]   ($ a year)
Σ_g p_g,d,t + u_d,t = D_d,t   (MW, every day and hour)
p_g,d,t ≤ a_g,d,t K_g   (a: output per MW built, 0 to 1)
symbols: a technology: wind, solar, gas combined-cycle (cc), gas peaker (pk)
a representative day, and an hour of it (t = 0 to 23, one hour each)
the days of the year that day d stands for
$ per MW of capacity per year
output in hour t of day d: a decision
MW (held for one hour, so also MWh)
output per MW built, 0 to 1 (wind and solar)
code: DAYS = {"winter": 121, "shoulder": 122, "summer": 122}       # days of 2025 each day stands for
weight = {d: DAYS[d] / 365 for d in DAYS}                    # share of the year
V = 10_000                                                    # $ per MWh of demand left unserved
minimize( sum(capital[g] * K[g] for g) + sum(weight[d] * (sum(cost[g] * p[g,d,t] for g) + V * u[d,t]) for d, t) )
for d, t: sum(p[g,d,t] for g) + u[d,t] == demand[d][t]                 # balance, MW
for g in ("wind", "solar"), d, t: p[g,d,t] <= avail[g][d][t] * K[g]   # output per MW built
for g in ("cc", "pk"), d, t: p[g,d,t] <= K[g]
report(K, annual_cost=objective, demand_in_year=sum(weight[d] * demand[d][t] for d, t))

days.label: Wednesday 2 April 2025
days.stands: April, May, October and November (122 days)

model.label: Model variant
model.short: Formulate and solve the water brief

tasksA.title: Your formulation
tasksA.prompt: Write your formulation of the water brief: sets, parameters with units, decision variables, the objective and every rule. A short version here is enough; keep the full one in your notebook.
points: Every parameter and variable has a unit: m³, m³ an hour, kWh per m³, $ per kWh, $ per kW.
The tower links the hours: the level at the end of an hour is the level an hour before, plus water pumped, minus water used.
The day's highest draw is a decision variable at least as large as every hour's pumping power, so the demand charge stays linear.
The day ends with at least the 2,000 m³ it started with, so the tower is not drained for free.
tasksA.solution: A [[linear-program|linear program]] with 49 variables: the water pumped and the tower's level in each hour, and the day's highest draw. The highest draw works like a capacity built in M3: one variable that every hour's draw must stay under.

tasksA.title: Least cost of the day
tasksA.prompt: Solve your model. What is the least electricity cost of the day, energy and demand charge together? Within 0.1% (about 50 cents) counts as right.
tasksA.solution: $526.90 for the day, energy and demand charge together. How it splits between them is in the worked solutions, which open once all eleven tasks are answered.

unitNote.kWh: kWh measures energy. The answer is a cost, in dollars.

tasksA.title: The highest draw
tasksA.prompt: In your least-cost schedule, what is the pumps' highest hourly draw of electricity? Within 0.5% (about 1 kW) counts as right.
tasksA.solution: 255 kW: the pumps run at 510 m³ an hour, well under their 900, because every kW of the day's highest draw costs $0.40.

unitNote.kWh: kWh measures energy. A draw is a rate of use: kW.
unitNote.m³ an hour: That is water. At 0.5 kWh per m³, convert the pumping rate to kW.

tasksA.title: Water pumped at the peak price
tasksA.prompt: How much water does your schedule pump in the five peak-price hours, 16:00 to 21:00? Within 1% (about 3 m³) counts as right.
tasksA.solution: 330 m³. To end the day at 2,000 m³ the tower must refill after the evening; pumping 330 m³ at the peak price costs less than raising the day's highest draw, which is charged once for every kW.

tasksA.title: A larger tower
tasksA.prompt: Solve again with a tower 100 m³ larger (4,100 m³). By how much does the day's cost fall? Within 2% (about 14 cents) counts as right.
tasksA.solution: About $6.83, or 6.8 cents a day for each m³ of extra room. The [[shadow-price|duals]] of the tower's upper limits, each the cost change from loosening that limit by one m³, add up to −$0.0683 per m³: the same saving over this step.

tasksC.title: Upper bound by hand
tasksC.prompt: Without the solver: what would the day cost if the pumps simply matched each hour's water use (pump as you go)? That plan is feasible, so the optimum cannot cost more. Within 0.5% (about $3.70) counts as right.
tasksC.solution: Energy: 0.5 kWh/m³ × each hour's use (m³) × its price ($/kWh), summed over the day = $601.80. Demand charge: the busiest hour draws 0.5 kWh/m³ × 650 m³ ÷ 1 h = 325 kW, × $0.40/kW = $130.00.

unitNote.kWh: kWh measures energy. The answer is a cost, in dollars.

tasksC.title: Lower bound by hand
tasksC.prompt: Without the solver: a lower bound, if every m³ could be pumped at the cheapest price and the draw spread evenly over the 24 hours. Within 0.5% (about $1.90) counts as right.

unitNote.kWh: kWh measures energy. The answer is a cost, in dollars.

tasksC.title: Your validation statement
tasksC.prompt: State whether your optimum lies between your two bounds, one special case your model reproduces exactly, and what these checks cannot show.
points: The optimum, $526.90, lies between the hand bounds, $375.67 and $731.80.

One clearly specified special case, matched exactly by an independent hand calculation; for example, with no demand charge and no limits on the tower or the pumps, the night price times the day's energy, $294.00 (another: one flat price and no demand charge).
Bounds and a special case show the model is plausible, not that its schedule is the cheapest; that rests on a correct formulation and the solver's optimality.
tasksC.solution: A [[validation|validation]] against hand calculations: the bounds bracket the optimum, and a special case is matched exactly.

tasksA.title: Your analysis design
tasksA.prompt: Write your design before computing: the question's type, the metrics with units, how you scale the data and pick the hours (with ties), and what the analysis leaves out.
points: A descriptive question with metrics in units: average output in the chosen hours, as a share of each farm's size and in MW.
The scaling stated: demand × 450 MW, wind × 150 MW, solar × 200 MW, so 100% means SPP's highest 2025 hour, not the farms' installed capacity.
The hours defined: the 100 highest by demand and by net load, the earlier hour first where values tie.
What it leaves out: one weather year, no outages and no [[resource-adequacy|adequacy]] calculation; an average over top hours is a screen, not a [[capacity-credit|capacity credit]].
tasksA.solution: A descriptive screen: averages over the year and over two sets of 100 hours, each with its unit and its definition written down before computing.

tasksA.title: Wind's mean output in the dataset
tasksA.prompt: In the dataset as scaled, what is the wind farm's mean output over 2025 as a percentage of its 150 MW, that is, of SPP's highest 2025 wind hour? Within 0.5% of the value (about 0.3 percentage points) counts as right.
tasksA.solution: 52.75%: the shape's mean over its maximum. It is a share of SPP's highest 2025 hour, not a capacity factor, which divides by installed capacity.

tasksA.title: Wind in the highest-demand hours
tasksA.prompt: What is the wind farm's average output in the 100 hours of highest demand, as a share of its 150 MW? Within 2% of the value (about 1.2 percentage points) counts as right.
tasksA.solution: 58.1%, a little above its year average: in 2025 the summer peaks of SPP demand came with some wind.

tasksA.title: Solar in the highest-demand hours
tasksA.prompt: And the solar farm's average output in the same 100 hours, as a share of its 200 MW? Within 2% of the value (about 1.4 percentage points) counts as right.
tasksA.solution: 69.0%: the highest-demand hours were summer afternoons and early evenings, between 12:00 and 21:00, while the sun was up.

tasksA.title: Both farms at net-load peaks
tasksA.prompt: In the 100 hours of highest net load (demand minus wind and solar), what do the two farms give together, on average? Within 2% (about 1 MW) counts as right.
tasksA.solution: 52.9 MW of their 350 MW: wind 29.6% and solar 4.3% of their sizes. The highest net-load hours are evenings, mostly 19:00 to 22:00, and winter nights and mornings: hours with little or no sun.

unitNote.MWh: MWh is energy. An average output is a power: MW.

tasksC.title: Against a published benchmark
tasksC.prompt: EIA reports a 2025 capacity factor of 33.8% for the U.S. utility-scale wind fleet. By how many percentage points does your figure from task 2 exceed it? Within 2% of the value (about 0.4 percentage points) counts as right.
tasksC.solution: 52.75% − 33.8% = 18.95 percentage points. The two figures divide by different things: the year's highest hour, and installed capacity.

tasksC.title: What the gap tells you
tasksC.prompt: What does that gap tell you?
options: The dataset is wrong and should not be used.
The dataset's percentages are shares of SPP's highest 2025 hour, not of capacity, and SPP's fleet and wind differ from the U.S. average; these data alone cannot split the gap between those causes.
Wind in 2025 was unusually strong everywhere.

why.a: No: the shapes are real and documented; the gap comes from what 100% means in them.
why.b: No: EIA's table is the primary national figure.
why.c: The benchmark exposes a definition, not an error, and the analysis must say which results depend on it.
why.d: Nothing in either source says so, and EIA's figure is the national average for 2025.

tasksC.solution: The dataset is normalised to its own highest hour, as its metadata say. Its mean output as a share of that hour is a different quantity from EIA's capacity factor, which divides by capacity: the comparison checks a definition, it does not validate the number.

tasksC.title: Your validation statement
tasksC.prompt: Name the benchmark and its date, read the gap, and say which of your results survive a rescaling of wind to EIA's 33.8% and which do not.
points: The benchmark named with its date: EIA, Electric Power Monthly, Table 6.07.B, 2025 annual: 33.8% for U.S. utility-scale wind.

The gap read as a definition difference (shares of the year's highest hour, not of capacity) plus a different fleet and region. The year file alone cannot separate them; if you use SPP's like-for-like capacity factor (Sources), say how it splits the gap and why the comparison is fair.

What survives a linear rescaling of wind to 33.8%, for the same 100 net-load hours: its ratio to its own average (about 0.56); the MW and the percentages do not. Picking the hours again after rescaling changes them (82 of 100 stay) and the ratio (0.71): say which you did.
tasksC.solution: A check against a published benchmark: it tests how the dataset's percentages are defined, not its values, which come from the same EIA-930 data. Then an honest note on which results depend on the scaling.

tasksB.title: The planted defect
tasksB.prompt: Run the supplied model (the button above, or the starter notebook) and read its code. Which line holds the planted defect?
options: Line 8: the wind and solar limits

why.a: The paper says each day stands for its days of the year; the code turns them into shares that sum to 1.
why.b: Those are annual costs per MW, in the same year as the objective. Look at what multiplies the running costs.
why.c: The objective's form matches the paper. Look at the values that go into it.
why.d: The limits match the paper: output per MW built times the capacity.

tasksB.solution: Line 2. With weights that sum to 1, the running costs of one average day meet a whole year of capital costs, so fuel looks almost free.

tasksB.title: The check that shows it
tasksB.prompt: Which line of the supplied model's report shows the defect most directly?

why.a: Suspicious, but a plan without wind or solar can be right when fuel is cheap; it does not show why.
why.b: Prairie Town uses about 2,470 GWh a year; the model's year holds 6,757 MWh, about one day.
why.c: That check passes here: each modelled hour balances.
why.d: Low or high compared with what? It needs a reference, such as the year's demand.

tasksB.solution: The year's total against an independent reference. 6,757 MWh is one average day of the town's 2,466 GWh in the model, or 2,469 GWh in the full 2025 data.

tasksB.title: The fixed model
tasksB.prompt: Fix the defect and solve again. What is the plan's annual cost? Within 0.5% (about $0.5 million) counts as right.
tasksB.solution: $106.8 million a year, about $43 per MWh of the 2,466 GWh: wind 548 MW, solar 211 MW, a gas combined-cycle plant of 152 MW and a 54 MW peaker, with no demand left unserved.

rubricLook: Your notebook reruns from top to bottom; your validation names its reference and its outcome; your defect report names the line, the check, the fix and the fixed number.
